summary: Describes how to carry text conversation sessions, as specified in ITU-T T.140, in RTP packets so people can chat in real time character by character. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level, and it was replaced by RFC 4103.

eli5.summary: Instead of waiting for a whole message, letters travel as you type, so the other person sees them appear live.

questions: how to send real time text over rtp
what is rtp payload for t.140
how does rtp handle text packet loss
subtitle: Sending typed text character-by-character over real-time protocols.

tldr.problem: Real-time text conversations need a way to send characters as they are typed, showing them live to the other person, and to recover from lost packets without waiting for a complete message.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2793 defines an RTP payload format that carries T.140 text (UTF-8 encoded) directly in RTP packets, with optional redundancy to protect against packet loss.
tldr.outcome: Text can now arrive character-by-character with loss detection and optional recovery, enabling live text chat alongside voice and video. This was replaced by RFC 4103.

today: RFC 2793 is a Proposed Standard from May 2000. It was replaced by RFC 4103, which updates this work with clarifications and improvements.

sections.title: Real-Time Text Conversation
sections.content:
RFC 2793 defines how to send text conversation in RTP packets, following the ITU-T T.140 standard. Text conversation differs from traditional chat: instead of waiting for the user to hit send, each character appears as it is typed, creating a live, interactive experience. This is especially valuable in multimedia sessions that already use voice and video.

Text is entered at a slow pace—a few characters per second—so each RTP packet usually carries just one new character (or a few). The RFC ensures that text arrives in the correct order, without duplicates, and marks where packets are lost.
sections.eli5: Real-time text lets the other person watch you type, letter by letter, instead of waiting for a message.

sections.title: T.140 and UTF-8 Encoding
sections.content:
The payload format is based on ITU-T T.140, which specifies how text conversation works. T.140 requires that all text and control elements be transmitted in ISO 10646 with UTF-8 encoding, making the protocol compatible with international scripts and modern systems.

A T.140 block is the unit of text in one RTP packet. Most of the time it is a single UTF-8-encoded character, but it can also be a sequence of characters or a control element (such as a backspace or a formatting change). Each block must contain a complete UTF-8 character; incomplete characters are not allowed.
sections.eli5: UTF-8 is a way to write any letter or symbol from any language using a code. Each character fits completely into a packet.

sections.title: RTP Packet Structure
sections.content:
A text conversation RTP packet contains an RTP header followed immediately by the T.140 data, with no additional framing. The RTP header includes:

  • Payload Type: Named T140 (or RED if redundancy is used).
  • Sequence Number: Incremented by one for each packet, used to detect loss and reordering.
  • Timestamp: Uses a clock frequency of 1000 Hz and marks when the text was entered. Sequential packets must have different timestamps.

When redundancy is enabled, the packet includes additional headers for each redundant block, each specifying a timestamp offset and length so the receiver can reconstruct lost text.
sections.eli5: The packet is like an envelope: it has a header with a number and a timestamp, then the text inside.

sections.title: Optional Redundancy
sections.content:
To reduce packet loss, the RFC allows redundant transmission following RFC 2198. A sender can include copies of text from recent previous packets. If a packet with new text is lost, the receiver may recover it from redundant data in a later packet.

The redundant blocks are placed in age order (oldest first), and all generations from the oldest retained back to the most recent must be included. This allows the receiver to infer sequence numbers and reassemble text correctly. The redundancy adds minimal overhead because RTP headers are much larger than the small amount of text in each packet.
sections.eli5: To protect against lost letters, you can send each letter twice in different packets. If one gets lost, the backup is still there.

sections.title: Receiving and Handling Loss
sections.content:
A receiver compares the sequence number of each new packet with the last correctly received packet. If the numbers are consecutive, the text is delivered immediately. If there is a gap, the receiver looks for redundant blocks in subsequent packets that fill the gap.

When text is missing and no redundancy is available, the receiver inserts a missing text marker (defined in T.140) so the user knows that some characters were lost. For packets that arrive out of order, the receiver can buffer them for up to 0.5 seconds to allow late packets to arrive and fill gaps.
sections.eli5: The receiver keeps track of which characters arrived. If one is missing, it marks the spot so the user sees there was a gap.
